title: Black Hole Jets Glow Brightest at Edges as Electrons Follow Magnetic Fields, Simulation Finds
excerpt: Black hole jets in Centaurus A glow brightest at their edges because electrons move along magnetic field lines, according to a German simulation published in Astronomy & Astrophysics. The model reproduces the Event Horizon Telescope image and puts the black hole near 60 million solar masses, though
content:
Astronomers at the University of Würzburg have used a computer simulation to reproduce how the black hole jet in the nearby galaxy Centaurus A looks in Event Horizon Telescope data, with the jet's edges glowing brighter than its center. The study, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, attributes the effect to electrons that move mostly along magnetic field lines instead of in all directions.

Centaurus A sits about 12 million light-years from Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope, a global network of radio dishes, imaged its jet base at a wavelength of 1.3 millimeters in a 2021 Nature Astronomy image built from 2017 observations. That image showed emission concentrated along the outer edges of the jet, a pattern called edge brightening or limb brightening, rather than along its axis.

The new work, led by Würzburg researchers with colleagues in Frankfurt, Turin, Shanghai, Nijmegen and Bonn, fits a physical model to that observation. According to a Würzburg release republished by Mirage News, lead author Glaser said Cen A is "our closest window into the physics of relativistic jets." The paper was posted on arXiv in March and published online Oct. 1.

How the simulation reproduces the image

The researchers ran a three-dimensional general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulation, which tracks plasma and magnetic fields around a spinning black hole. They then converted its output into synthetic radio images and compared those with the Event Horizon Telescope measurements using Bayesian fitting. The best-fitting model reproduced the edge-brightened look of the observed jet.

The key ingredient is an anisotropy parameter, called eta, that compares electron pressure across magnetic field lines with pressure along them. A value of 1 means electrons move equally in all directions. The fit prefers 0.07, so pressure across the field lines is roughly 14 times weaker than along them, a strong departure from isotropy.

The paper's explanation runs through the jet's structure. Its central spine is dilute and strongly magnetized, so electrons there lose energy faster. Electrons that travel mostly along the field radiate less strongly at large angles to the field, which shifts brightness from the spine to the surrounding sheath. The same fit puts the black hole's mass near 60 million times that of the Sun, above the earlier estimate of about 55 million, and favors a magnetically arrested disk, a state where magnetic flux piles up near the black hole.

Where magnetic reconnection fits

Magnetic reconnection is a process in which magnetic field lines break and rejoin, converting stored magnetic energy into heat and fast particles. Particle-in-cell simulations by Luca Comisso and Brian Jiang of Columbia University found that pitch-angle anisotropy imprinted by reconnection can arise in accelerated electrons, which is the kind of directional bias the Centaurus A model needs.

That makes reconnection a natural candidate for the cause, but the Centaurus A fit constrains the anisotropy itself and does not by itself identify its source. Treat the reconnection link as a well-motivated hypothesis rather than a proven mechanism.

Open questions and limits

The model does not match everything. The best fit implies a viewing angle of about 72 degrees, which the authors call significantly larger than the 12 to 45 degrees suggested by lower-frequency studies, though it agrees with other estimates of 50 to 80 degrees. The authors note that the tension is unresolved and could hint at a bend in the jet.

The authors also report leftover discrepancies in the data near 3.5 gigalambda on baselines involving the Large Millimeter Telescope, a jet base more compact than in the observed images, and a lower polarization fraction in the model. They list a denser ambient medium, alternative magnetic field shapes and an expanded Event Horizon Telescope array as next steps.

What comes next

The model also makes a prediction: the black hole's shadow in Centaurus A should become visible at about 3 terahertz, and the paper names the proposed space-based interferometers BHEX and SHARP as ways to test it. On the ground, the National Radio Astronomy Observatory has announced a pathfinder for the next-generation array of 263 planned antennas. The Square Kilometre Array also publishes an SKA science verification timeline, with early science verification for its low-frequency array anticipated in the first half of 2027. Neither facility is part of the Würzburg study.

A separate Würzburg-linked effort, the Wetterstein Millimeter Telescope, is planned for the Zugspitzplatt near Germany's highest peak at roughly 2,500 meters, but it has not been built.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Centaurus A?

Centaurus A is a galaxy about 12 million light-years away that hosts the nearest radio galaxy to Earth, according to the Event Horizon Telescope and Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy. Its radio structure spans about eight degrees of sky, roughly 16 times the Moon's angular diameter. It was identified as one of the first known extragalactic radio sources in 1949.

Why are black hole jets brighter at the edges?

In the new model, electrons in the dilute, strongly magnetized central spine lose energy faster, and electrons moving mostly along magnetic field lines radiate less toward the observer from the spine. Brightness shifts to the surrounding sheath at the jet's borders, which matches what the Event Horizon Telescope saw in Centaurus A.

What is magnetic reconnection?

Magnetic reconnection is a process in which magnetic field lines break and reconnect, releasing stored magnetic energy and accelerating charged particles. Simulations suggest it can leave electrons with a preferred direction of motion along the field.

Can astronomers see the shadow of the Centaurus A black hole?

Not yet. The 2021 image resolved the jet's base, not the black hole's shadow. The new study predicts the shadow should appear at about 3 terahertz, a frequency that would need higher-resolution instruments, such as the space-based concepts BHEX and SHARP named in the paper.
